caption:
Sakana AI's new Fugu Ultra ships with a benchmark chart next to Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos Preview. Neither model was in the room for the test. Sakana says so itself: baseline scores are provider-reported, and Fable 5 and Mythos Preview never touched Fugu's pool because they weren't publicly reachable when the chart went live.

Here's what Fugu actually is: not a new frontier model, but an API that reads your prompt, farms it out to a pool of other companies' models, chains a few together, and hands you back one answer like a single system did the work. Sakana built it on its own ICLR 2026 research (Trinity and Conductor), and it's already routable on OpenRouter and listed in the Nous Research portal next to every other model on the shelf.

One place Sakana does publish a direct number against Fable 5: SWE-Bench Pro. Fable 5 still wins, 80.0 to Fugu Ultra's 73.7. That's the number to sit with before anyone signs off on an orchestrator because the chart looked good. You also can't see which vendor's model handled a given prompt, or log that the way you'd log any other subprocessor.

The thesis is direct: a benchmark-topping chart is marketing, not an audit. Before an orchestrator like this touches production data, get the provider list, confirm per-call logging, and put it on the same vendor risk register as every other subprocessor you use.

Would you sign off on an API that won't say which model just read your data? Tell me below.

Follow for AI security breakdowns without the fake panic.
comment_prompt: Would your team route sensitive prompts through an API that won't disclose which underlying model answered each call? What would you need to see first?
alt_text: Sakana claims its Fugu Ultra AI matches Anthropic's best model, but never tested against it directly. A sealed envelope splits open to reveal smaller identical envelopes spilling out beneath it.
Sakana AI released Fugu and Fugu Ultra as one API that routes prompts through other companies' models. A conductor's baton rests across a row of six different instrument cases in the dark.
Fugu Ultra's benchmark chart lists two models that were never actually in its testing pool. An empty velvet pedestal sits under a spotlight beside a folded printed scoreboard.

Sakana's own published benchmark chart, screenshotted directly from its release page: Fugu Ultra and Fugu compared against Fable 5, Mythos Preview, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5, and Opus 4.8 across eight benchmarks.
Fugu picks and chains other language models per task, then merges the results into one answer. A relay baton passes hand to hand through a chain of blurred running figures in the dark.

Teams adopt AI orchestrators on benchmark charts alone and skip asking which vendor's model actually handled their data. An unmarked shipping crate is wheeled past an open, unattended checkpoint gate.
The fix: log every orchestrator call and add it to your vendor risk register like any other subprocessor. A row of wax seals is pressed one by one onto a stack of dark folders under a desk lamp.
The chart proves the compared model was already gone, not that Fugu Ultra beat it. A single cracked trophy cup sits alone in deep negative space with a long shadow.
Closing question: would you sign off on an API that won't say which model read your data? A clean dark end card holds empty space for the question and handle.

narration.text: Sakana AI just told the world its new model matches Anthropic's best system, and it never got the chance to actually test against it.
Fugu Ultra is not one trained model. It is an API that quietly routes your prompt through a pool of other companies' systems and answers as if it were one.
Before you plug something like that into production, get its provider list, confirm it logs every call, and put the whole thing on your vendor risk register.
That benchmark chart does not prove Fugu Ultra beat the model it is compared against. It proves that model was already pulled from public access.
So would you trust an API that will not say which model just read your data? Tell me in the comments, and follow for more of this.
